q: Ames transferred land with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to a newly formed corporation in exchange for stock worth $80,000 and $20,000 cash. Immediately afterward Ames owned 85% of the corporation's only class of stock. How much gain must Ames recognize?
exp: Realized gain is $100,000 − $30,000 = $70,000, but under §351 gain is recognized only to the extent of boot received, so the recognized gain is the lesser of $70,000 or the $20,000 cash. Recognizing the full $70,000 ignores §351 nonrecognition, which applies because Ames has 80% control.

q: Using the same facts (land basis $30,000, FMV $100,000, exchanged for $80,000 of stock and $20,000 cash in a qualifying §351 transfer, $20,000 gain recognized), what is Ames's basis in the stock received?
exp: Under §358, stock basis = $30,000 property basis + $20,000 gain recognized − $20,000 cash received = $30,000. Using the stock's $80,000 fair market value is the common mistake; the deferred $50,000 gain is preserved in the lower basis.

q: Wade transferred machinery with an adjusted basis of $45,000 and a fair market value of $90,000 to his controlled corporation for stock worth $75,000 and $15,000 cash in a transaction qualifying under §351. What is the corporation's basis in the machinery?
exp: Wade recognizes gain equal to the $15,000 boot (realized gain $45,000), and the corporation's basis is the transferor's basis plus gain recognized: $45,000 + $15,000 = $60,000 (§362). The corporation does not take a $90,000 fair market value basis in a §351 transfer.

q: Baker transferred a building with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $150,000, subject to a $60,000 mortgage, to a corporation in exchange for all of its stock. The corporation assumed the mortgage, and there was no tax-avoidance purpose. How much gain does Baker recognize?
exp: Under §357, liabilities assumed in excess of the aggregate basis of property transferred produce gain: $60,000 − $40,000 = $20,000. Liability assumption is normally not boot, so answering $0 overlooks the excess-liability rule.

q: Cole transferred equipment with an adjusted basis of $80,000 and a fair market value of $200,000, subject to a $50,000 liability, to a corporation for stock worth $150,000. The corporation assumed the liability, Cole has 100% control, and there was a bona fide business purpose. What is Cole's basis in the stock?
exp: No gain is recognized because the $50,000 liability does not exceed the $80,000 basis, but the liability assumed is treated as money received for basis purposes: $80,000 − $50,000 = $30,000 (§358). Ignoring the liability gives $80,000.

q: Dahl transferred property worth $70,000 to a new corporation for 70 shares, and Eng received 30 shares worth $30,000 solely for services rendered in organizing the corporation. These were the only shares issued. What is the tax result?
choices: Neither Dahl nor Eng recognizes income because §351 applies to the incorporation
Dahl recognizes his realized gain on the property, and Eng recognizes $30,000 of ordinary income
Dahl recognizes no gain, and Eng recognizes $30,000 of ordinary income
Dahl recognizes no gain, and Eng recognizes $30,000 of capital gain
exp: Stock received solely for services is not counted toward the 80% control test, so the property transferors own only 70% and §351 fails; Dahl's realized gain is taxable. Eng has $30,000 of ordinary compensation income in any event.

q: For purposes of §351, control means ownership immediately after the exchange of stock possessing at least:
choices: 50% of the voting power and 50% of the value of all stock
80% of the total value of all classes of stock
80% of the total combined voting power and 80% of the total number of shares of each class of nonvoting stock
More than 50% of the voting power of all classes of stock
exp: Section 368 defines control as at least 80% of the total combined voting power of all voting stock and at least 80% of the total number of shares of each other class of stock. The test is not based on the value of the stock.

q: Which statement about holding periods in a §351 transfer of a capital asset in exchange for stock only is correct?
choices: The shareholder's holding period in the stock begins on the date of the exchange
The corporation's holding period in the asset begins on the date of the exchange
Neither the shareholder nor the corporation may tack a prior holding period
The shareholder tacks the asset's holding period onto the stock, and the corporation tacks the shareholder's holding period onto the asset
exp: Stock received for a capital or §1231 asset takes a holding period that includes the asset's holding period (§1223(1)), and the corporation's carryover-basis property includes the transferor's holding period (§1223(2)). Tacking for the shareholder would not apply if the property were inventory.

q: Fern Corp. issued 1,000 shares of its own newly issued common stock in exchange for land worth $250,000. Fern's shares had no prior basis. How much gain does Fern Corp. recognize?
choices: $0, because a corporation recognizes no gain or loss on issuing its own stock for property
$250,000, because Fern's basis in its new shares is zero
$250,000 of capital gain, deferred until Fern sells the land
Gain equal to the excess of the land's value over its par value
exp: Under §1032 a corporation recognizes no gain or loss on receiving money or property in exchange for its own stock, whether or not §351 applies to the transferor. The zero basis of newly issued shares is irrelevant.

q: Gray transferred property to her controlled corporation, and the corporation assumed a liability that Gray had incurred shortly before the transfer for the principal purpose of avoiding federal income tax. How is the liability treated?
choices: It is ignored for both gain and basis purposes
The entire liability is treated as money received (boot) by Gray
Only the portion of the liability exceeding Gray's basis is treated as boot
It is treated as a contribution to capital by the corporation
exp: Under the §357 tax-avoidance rule, if the principal purpose of a liability assumption is tax avoidance or lacks a bona fide business purpose, the total amount of all liabilities assumed is treated as money received. The excess-over-basis rule is a separate provision of §357.

q: Hale transferred equipment with an adjusted basis of $100,000 and a fair market value of $70,000 to a corporation solely for stock in a transaction qualifying under §351. Hale made no election under §362(e)(2)(C). What is the corporation's basis in the equipment?
exp: When the aggregate basis of property a transferor contributes exceeds its aggregate fair market value, §362(e)(2) limits the corporation's basis to fair market value, $70,000, while Hale keeps a $100,000 stock basis. A $100,000 carryover basis would duplicate the built-in loss.

q: Ivey transferred property with an adjusted basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 to her controlled corporation for stock worth $30,000 and $10,000 cash. What is Ivey's basis in the stock?
exp: No loss is recognized in a §351 exchange even when boot is received (§351), so stock basis = $50,000 − $10,000 cash + $0 gain = $40,000. Using the stock's $30,000 value incorrectly treats the transaction as taxable.

q: Jory transferred land (basis $10,000, FMV $40,000) and also performed services worth $10,000 in exchange for stock worth $50,000. Jory's transfer of property qualifies under §351. What is Jory's basis in the stock?
exp: Jory recognizes $10,000 of ordinary income for the stock received for services, and that income is added to basis: $10,000 land basis + $10,000 compensation income = $20,000. The $30,000 gain on the land is deferred, so using full value of $50,000 is wrong.

q: Kim owns all 100 outstanding shares of Kay Corp. Lee transfers appreciated property to Kay Corp. for 150 newly issued shares; Kim transfers nothing. What is the tax consequence to Lee?
choices: No gain, because Kay Corp. is controlled by its shareholders after the exchange
Lee recognizes his realized gain, because the transferors own only 60% immediately after the exchange
No gain, because §351 applies whenever new shares are issued for property
Lee recognizes gain only to the extent his shares exceed 50% of the stock
exp: Only stock held by transferors counts toward control; Lee owns 150 ÷ 250 = 60%, short of 80%, so the exchange is taxable to Lee. Kim could be counted only by also transferring property of more than relatively small value.

q: Lund transferred equipment with an original cost of $50,000, an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $45,000 to his controlled corporation for stock worth $40,000 and $5,000 cash. What is the amount and character of Lund's recognized gain?
choices: $25,000 ordinary income
$5,000 capital gain
$5,000 ordinary income
exp: Recognized gain is limited to the $5,000 boot (realized gain $25,000), and because recognized gain does not exceed the $30,000 of prior depreciation, it is ordinary §1245 recapture. The unrecognized recapture carries over to the corporation.

q: A married couple filing jointly sold §1244 stock they had acquired at original issuance for $180,000 for $30,000. The corporation met all §1244 requirements. How is the $150,000 loss treated?
choices: $150,000 ordinary loss
$3,000 ordinary loss and $147,000 capital loss carryover
$50,000 ordinary loss and $100,000 capital loss
$100,000 ordinary loss and $50,000 capital loss
exp: Section 1244 allows an ordinary loss of up to $100,000 per year on a joint return ($50,000 for other filers); the remaining $50,000 is capital loss. Reversing the two amounts applies the single-filer limit to the wrong portion.

q: Which statement about §1244 stock is correct?
choices: Only an individual (or partnership) that acquired the stock at original issuance from the corporation may claim the ordinary loss
Any later purchaser of the stock may claim the ordinary loss
A corporate shareholder may claim the ordinary loss
Gain on the sale of §1244 stock is also ordinary
exp: The §1244 ordinary loss is available only to the original individual holder (or a partnership that was the original holder, passed through to individual partners) of stock issued for money or property. Gains on §1244 stock remain capital, and later purchasers and corporations do not qualify.

q: In a transaction otherwise qualifying under §351, Mona received stock and a 10-year note issued by the corporation. How is the note treated?
choices: As stock, because it is a long-term security
As boot, taxable to the extent of Mona's realized gain
As a nontaxable return of capital
As ordinary income equal to its face amount
exp: Since 1989, §351 protects only stock; debt securities of any term are boot, and gain is recognized up to their value (with possible installment reporting). Treating long-term securities as stock reflects pre-1989 law.

q: In a §351 exchange, Nash Corp. transferred land it held (basis $5,000, FMV $15,000) to a transferor as part of the consideration, along with Nash stock. What does Nash Corp. recognize?
choices: No gain, because §1032 protects the corporation
No gain, because the land is boot only to the shareholder
$10,000 gain, because a corporation recognizes gain on transferring appreciated property other than its own stock
$15,000 gain equal to the land's fair market value
exp: Section 351 applies §311 rules, so the corporation recognizes gain on appreciated boot property it transfers: $15,000 − $5,000 = $10,000. Section 1032 covers only the corporation's own stock.

q: Ortiz, the sole shareholder of Ortiz Corp., contributed $40,000 cash to the corporation without receiving any additional shares. Which statement is correct?
choices: The corporation has $40,000 of gross income
Ortiz may deduct the $40,000 as a business expense
Ortiz must recognize gain because no stock was received
The corporation excludes the contribution, and Ortiz increases the basis of her existing shares by $40,000
exp: A shareholder's contribution to capital is excluded from the corporation's income under §118 and is added to the shareholder's basis in existing stock. Receiving no new shares does not make the contribution taxable or deductible.

q: Pell Corp., a calendar-year corporation, began business on July 1 and incurred $52,000 of qualifying organizational expenditures. It elects the maximum current deduction and amortizes the rest. What is its total deduction for organizational expenditures for the first year?
exp: The immediate deduction is $5,000 reduced by the $2,000 excess over $50,000, or $3,000; the remaining $49,000 is amortized over 180 months: $49,000 ÷ 180 × 6 = $1,633, for a total of $4,633. Taking the full $5,000 ignores the dollar-for-dollar phase-down.

q: Which cost incurred in forming a corporation is NOT an organizational expenditure eligible for deduction and amortization under §248?
choices: Legal fees for drafting the corporate charter and bylaws
Commissions paid to underwriters for selling the corporation's stock
State incorporation fees
Fees for accounting services incident to organization
exp: Costs of issuing or selling stock, such as underwriting commissions and printing stock certificates, reduce paid-in capital and are neither deductible nor amortizable. Charter, incorporation and organizational accounting and legal fees qualify under §248.

q: Quinn transferred property with a fair market value of $60,000 and an adjusted basis of $90,000 to his controlled corporation. He would prefer to recognize the $30,000 loss. Which statement is correct?
choices: Quinn may elect out of §351 to recognize the loss
Quinn recognizes the loss because §351 applies only to gains
Quinn cannot recognize the loss, because §351 is mandatory when its requirements are met
Quinn recognizes half the loss and defers the rest
exp: Section 351 is not elective; if the property, stock and 80% control requirements are met, both gain and loss are deferred. A taxpayer wanting the loss would need to structure a transaction that fails §351, such as a sale.

q: Fay transferred land (basis $60,000, FMV $100,000) for 50 shares of a new corporation, and Gus transferred $90,000 cash and services worth $10,000 for the other 50 shares. What is Gus's basis in his shares?
exp: Gus's shares count toward control because the property he contributed is not of relatively small value, so §351 applies to both transferors. Gus has $10,000 of ordinary income and a basis of $90,000 cash + $10,000 income = $100,000.

q: Rios, a cash-basis sole proprietor, incorporated her business by transferring accounts receivable (basis $0, FMV $30,000) and equipment (basis $20,000) to a corporation for all its stock. The corporation assumed $35,000 of trade accounts payable that would be deductible when paid. How much gain does Rios recognize?
exp: Liabilities whose payment would give rise to a deduction are excluded under §357 when testing whether liabilities exceed basis, so no gain arises even though $35,000 exceeds the $20,000 basis. Applying the excess-liability rule without the exclusion gives $15,000.

q: Seth transferred property with a basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $120,000, subject to a $30,000 liability, to his controlled corporation for stock worth $80,000 plus $10,000 cash; the corporation assumed the liability with a bona fide business purpose. What is Seth's basis in the stock?
exp: Seth recognizes $10,000 gain (the cash; the liability is not boot). Stock basis = $50,000 + $10,000 gain − $10,000 cash − $30,000 liability = $20,000. Forgetting to subtract the liability gives $50,000.

q: Tate transferred property with a basis of $25,000 and a fair market value of $90,000, subject to a $40,000 mortgage, to her wholly owned corporation for stock. The corporation assumed the mortgage for a bona fide business purpose. What is the corporation's basis in the property?
exp: Tate recognizes $40,000 − $25,000 = $15,000 of gain under §357, and the corporation's basis is $25,000 + $15,000 = $40,000. The corporation does not take a fair market value basis.

q: Which statement about §351 is correct?
choices: It applies only to the formation of a new corporation
It requires each transferor individually to own at least 80% of the stock
It applies only when transferors receive voting common stock
It can apply to transfers to an existing corporation if the transferors as a group have control immediately afterward
exp: Section 351 applies to transfers to new or existing corporations; the 80% control test is applied to all transferors in the transaction as a group, and any class of stock qualifies. Individual 80% ownership is not required.

q: Which of the following is NOT treated as property for purposes of §351?
choices: Services rendered to the corporation
Cash
Accounts receivable of a cash-basis taxpayer
A patent or secret process
exp: Section 351 excludes services from the definition of property, so stock received for services is taxable compensation and does not count toward control. Cash, receivables and intangibles are all property.

q: Uma and Vic transferred property to a new corporation for 100% of its stock. Under a binding agreement made before the exchange, Uma immediately sold enough of her shares to an unrelated buyer that the transferors' combined ownership fell to 70%. What is the likely result?
choices: Section 351 applies because control existed for an instant after the exchange
Section 351 fails because the prearranged sale means the transferors lacked control immediately after the exchange
Only Uma is taxed, because only she sold shares
The sale is ignored because it was to an unrelated buyer
exp: Control must exist immediately after the exchange, and a binding prearranged disposition of stock is taken into account under the step-transaction doctrine, so the transferors are treated as owning only 70%. Momentary ownership does not satisfy the test.
